rows.n: Kanda Myōjin (神田明神)
rows.w: 1,300-year-old shrine of Edo's merchants, home of the Kanda Matsuri — and, a block from Akihabara, an anime pilgrimage stop (Love Live!) with IT-blessing omamori.

rows.n: Akihabara Electric Town (秋葉原電気街)
rows.w: Tokyo's electronics-and-otaku quarter — multi-storey arcades, figure shops, retro-game dens and maid cafés around Chūō-dōri.

rows.n: Mandarake Complex Akihabara (まんだらけコンプレックス)
rows.nat: まんだらけコンプレックス
rows.w: Eight-storey flagship of the second-hand otaku chain, each floor sorted by product type — vintage 'Japanese Pop Antique' figures, magical-girl toys and cosplay, manga, dōjinshi and more (Time Out, Tokyo Cheapo).

rows.n: Tokyo Character Street, Tokyo Station (東京キャラクターストリート)
rows.nat: 東京キャラクターストリート
rows.w: An underground row of 30-plus official character shops opened in 2008 on the Yaesu side of Tokyo Station — Pokémon, Studio Ghibli, Kirby, Chiikawa, Crayon Shin-chan, Rilakkuma and Hello Kitty, some with station-exclusive goods.

rows.n: Akihabara Radio Kaikan (秋葉原ラジオ会館)
rows.w: Akihabara's ten floors of otaku culture by the station — figures, trading cards, model kits, gacha machines and K-Books.

rows.n: Super Potato Akihabara (スーパーポテト 秋葉原店)
rows.nat: スーパーポテト 秋葉原店
rows.w: Three floors of retro consoles, cartridges and memorabilia in a Mario-decorated building; Time Out calls the Akihabara flagship the chain's most famous location, 'almost like a museum'.

rows.n: Pokémon Café Tokyo, Nihonbashi (ポケモンカフェ 日本橋)
rows.nat: ポケモンカフェ 日本橋
rows.w: The world's first Pokémon Café (2018), beside Pokémon Center Tokyo DX; reopened 17 June 2026 after renovation with Pikachu curry, Eevee pancakes, the new Pika Pika Parfait and a live Chef Pikachu show — the Gengar smoothie stays.

rows.n: Suga Shrine stairs, Yotsuya (須賀神社 男坂)
rows.w: The stone 'Otokozaka' staircase below Suga Shrine is where Taki and Mitsuha finally meet in the last scene of Shinkai Makoto's Your Name (2016) and on its poster; nippon.com calls it among the most famous seichi-junrei sites in Japan. Nearest station Yotsuya-sanchōme.
ph: The stairs below Suga Shrine, Yotsuya
“Suga Shrine stairs low-angle 20161113-071158” by Hisagi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons — resized to 500 and 960 px wide

rows.n: Tokyu Kabukichō Tower (東急歌舞伎町タワー)
rows.w: 2023 entertainment tower in the heart of Kabukichō — theatre, a neon 'Shinjuku Kabuki Hall' food hall of yokochō stalls and rooftop views; the Godzilla head looms next door.

rows.n: Godzilla Head, Hotel Gracery Shinjuku (ゴジラヘッド)
rows.w: A life-size Godzilla head glowering over Kabukichō from the Shinjuku Tōhō Building's 8th-floor terrace — it roars and glows on the hour.

rows.n: Nintendo TOKYO & Pokémon Center Shibuya (Shibuya PARCO 6F)
rows.w: 'Cyberspace Shibuya' on PARCO's 6th floor — Nintendo's only official Tokyo store beside the Pokémon Center with its life-size Mewtwo; expect queues.

rows.n: Tokyo Anime Center, DNP Plaza Shibuya (東京アニメセンター)
rows.w: Formerly in Akihabara and then Ichigaya, the Tokyo Anime Center now runs rotating anime, manga and game exhibitions with AR/VR on the second floor of DNP Plaza Shibuya; the shop is free to enter.

rows.n: Isegen (いせ源)
rows.w: Tokyo's only anko-nabe specialist, cooking monkfish hotpot since 1830 in a 1930 wooden house — no reservations, no cards, open in the cold season.

rows.n: Virtù, Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi
rows.w: Art-deco cocktail bar at the Four Seasons Otemachi; the Virtù Martini uses Japanese gin and vodka with hinoki bitters. Asia's 50 Best Bars 2026 No 26 and World's 50 Best Bars 2025.

rows.n: Hibiya Park (日比谷公園)
rows.w: Japan's first Western-style park (1903), across the moat from the Imperial Palace — rose beds, an open-air concert hall and the century-old Matsumoto-rō restaurant.

rows.n: National Diet Building (国会議事堂)
rows.w: The stepped-pyramid granite parliament (1936) — free guided tours of the House of Councillors chamber run on weekdays.

rows.n: Jimbōchō Book Town (神保町古書店街)
rows.w: 100+ second-hand and antiquarian bookshops along Yasukuni-dōri — named Time Out's World's Coolest Neighbourhood 2025; also a curry-rice heartland.

rows.n: Tokyo International Forum (東京国際フォーラム)
rows.w: Rafael Viñoly's 1996 glass-hull atrium between Yūrakuchō and Tokyo Station — free to walk through, with a weekend antique market on the plaza.

rows.n: Kitanomaru Park (北の丸公園)
rows.w: Wooded former Edo Castle enclosure north of the palace — the Budōkan, the Science Museum and MOMAT among cherry trees by the Chidorigafuchi moat.

rows.n: Akihabara Radio Kaikan (秋葉原ラジオ会館)
rows.w: Akihabara's ten floors of otaku culture by the station — figures, trading cards, model kits, gacha machines and K-Books.

rows.n: Tokyo Daijingū (東京大神宮)
rows.w: The Tokyo branch of Ise, where the first Shintō wedding was held in 1901 — now the city's favourite shrine for praying for love, with matchmaking omikuji.

rows.n: Marunouchi Building (丸の内ビルディング)
rows.w: The 'Maru-biru' facing Tokyo Station — free 5th-floor terrace views over the restored station dome and restaurant floors up to the 36th.

rows.n: Nippon Budōkan (日本武道館)
rows.w: The octagonal 1964 Olympic judo hall that became Japan's rock temple (the Beatles, 1966) — still the martial-arts and concert landmark of Kitanomaru Park.

rows.n: Mitsubishi Ichigōkan Museum (三菱一号館美術館)
rows.w: A faithful 2009 rebuild of Josiah Conder's 1894 red-brick Mitsubishi office, now a museum of 19th-century European art beside the Brick Square garden.

rows.n: National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo (MOMAT)
rows.w: Japan's first national art museum — the definitive collection of 20th-century Japanese painting (Kishida, Yokoyama Taikan) beside the palace moat.

rows.n: Science Museum, Kitanomaru (科学技術館)
rows.w: Hands-on Japan Science Foundation museum in Kitanomaru Park — five floors of experiments, bikes, robots and electricity shows for kids.

rows.n: Seikadō Bunko Art Museum (静嘉堂文庫美術館)
rows.w: The Iwasaki family's treasure collection — including a National Treasure yōhen tenmoku tea bowl — now shown in the 1934 Meiji Seimei-kan in Marunouchi.

rows.n: National Shōwa Memorial Museum — Shōwa-kan (昭和館)
rows.w: Museum of everyday life in wartime and postwar Japan (1935–1955) — ration books, school bags, black-market goods and the home front, by Kudanshita Station.

rows.n: Tsukiji Hongan-ji (築地本願寺)
rows.w: Startling 1934 Indian-style Buddhist temple by Itō Chūta, with a pipe organ inside and a breakfast café — at the gate of the Tsukiji outer market.

rows.n: Kabuki-za (歌舞伎座)
rows.w: Tokyo's grand kabuki theatre behind a Momoyama-style facade — buy a single-act makumi ticket on the day to sample a play from the top gallery.

rows.n: Meiji Jingū Gaien & Ichō Namiki Ginkgo Avenue (明治神宮外苑 いちょう並木)
rows.nat: 明治神宮外苑 いちょう並木
rows.w: The Outer Garden's 300 m double row of 146 ginkgo trees that turns pure gold in late November — Tokyo's most famous autumn avenue, leading to the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery.

rows.n: Tokyo Midtown (東京ミッドタウン)
rows.w: Roppongi's 2007 complex on the old Defence Agency site — Hinokichō Park, the galleria and two design museums in its grounds.

rows.n: Institute for Nature Study (国立科学博物館附属自然教育園)
rows.nat: 国立科学博物館附属自然教育園
rows.w: A fenced-off fragment of primeval Musashino forest and marsh near Meguro Station — admission is capped so the trails stay quiet.

rows.n: Kyū-Shiba-rikyū Gardens (旧芝離宮恩賜庭園)
rows.w: One of Tokyo's oldest daimyō stroll gardens (1678), a pond landscape tucked beside Hamamatsuchō Station.

rows.n: Odaiba Marine Park (お台場海浜公園)
rows.w: Artificial beach on Tokyo Bay facing Rainbow Bridge and the skyline — a mini Statue of Liberty, sunset strolls and the night view back over the water.

rows.n: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden (新宿御苑)
rows.w: Former imperial garden blending French formal, English landscape and Japanese styles — 1,000 cherry trees, a tropical greenhouse and a teahouse, minutes from Shinjuku Station.
